To produce e-methanol, syngas is first produced from renewable hydrogen and captured CO from a point source via a RWGS, then directed to methanol synthesis 2 (Zang et al. 2021). 2.2 TECHNOECONOMIC ANALYSIS (TEA) The TEA was performed with consistent economic assumptions based on the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE’s) Bioenergy Technologies Office guidelines (Snowden-Swan et al., 2022b). Mass and energy balances and equipment cost for selected pathways are derived from existing process models or literature, as described in Section 2.1. Subsequently, a discounted cash-flow analysis was conducted to determine the minimum fuel selling price (MFSP), which must achieve a 10% internal rate of return and a net present value of zero. All costs were adjusted to 2020 U.S. dollars, and MFSPs were expressed in dollars per diesel gallon equivalent (DGE). Note that the selected fuel pathways use various conversion technologies with differing TRLs and feedstocks, and raw materials, which results in varying levels of uncertainty in the modeled MFSPs presented in Section 2.2.2. For fair comparison, technoeconomic uncertainty in this study was quantified for the selected pathways based on their state-of-technology as of 2024. The lower or 6 upper bound of the analysis results reflects a possible range based on current technological performance, which is subject to change with continuous R&D. The key TEA model inputs selected for this study were utility prices, the most significant variable cost contributors, process performance, and capital costs. Five-year historical data were used to define utility, feedstock, and raw material prices. Uncertainties related to process performance and capital costs are heavily influenced by the TRLs of the conversion pathways. Process models for pathways with a TRL greater than 5 are expected to be more accurate, resulting in smaller deviations for fuel yield (±5% versus ±10%) and utility consumptions (±10% versus ±20%). The uncertainties of capital cost also decrease with increasing TRL, as high TRL technologies will have a more well-defined capital project and have been proven by piloting or commercial practices (+15%/-10% for TRLs >8; +30%/-20% for TRLs 5–7; and +50%/-30% for TRLs <5). 2.2.1 Modeled MFSP Figure 2-1 shows the modeled MFSP in dollars per DGE for the 16 selected alternative fuel pathways. It is important to note that the MFSP shown here does not account for potential incentive programs available at the federal and state levels. Technology and market uncertainties as well as impacts of incentive programs on MFSP are discussed in Sections 2.2.2 and 2.2.3. As mentioned in Section 2.1, BD and RD from soybean oil are currently available in the U.S. fuel market. The modeled MFSPs for BD and RD from soybean oil are $3.51 and $4.03 per DGE ($3.26 and $3.85/gallon), respectively. These are comparable to the U.S. BD price of $3.08–3.73/gallon and the California RD price of $3.10–3.76/gallon in 2020 (DOE, 2025).
